support_filament_matching.tooltip: When enabled, support material matches the filament of the model it touches or stands beside: interfaces and ironing take the color of the surface they support, and support walls near a painted wall take that wall's color. Reduces color contamination between supports and the model. Any support geometry left over after matching keeps the color already assigned to it and will not be repainted by Flush into objects' support.

support_interface_not_for_body.label: Avoid interface filament for base
support_interface_not_for_body.tooltip: Avoid using support interface filament to print support base if possible.

support_interface_interlock.label: Interlock interface with support body
support_interface_interlock.tooltip:
When the support interface is printed in a different filament from the support body, weave the interface layers under the top one into the body: they are cut into stripes that alternate the body and the interface filament, and each layer's stripes are turned 90 degrees from the layer below. The interface then cannot peel off the body. The top interface layer, the one that touches the model, is not changed.
Applies to the top interfaces of normal and tree supports (all tree styles). Needs at least one top interface layer more than the woven layers. Not used when "Support Filament Matching" is on.

support_interface_interlock_layers.label: Woven layers
support_interface_interlock_layers.tooltip:
Number of interface layers under the top one that are woven into the support body. Top interface layers must be at least this plus one.
With exactly one more top interface layer, the bottom (bonding) layer is woven too, which adds about 2 filament changes per height where a support roof starts on single-nozzle printers. With two or more extra layers and a non-soluble interface the weave adds no filament changes.

support_interface_interlock_beam_lines.label: Stripe width
support_interface_interlock_beam_lines.tooltip: Width of each woven stripe, in support lines. Islands narrower than two stripes are not woven.

support_ironing.label: Ironing Support Interface
support_ironing.tooltip: Ironing is using small flow to print on same height of support interface again to make it more smooth. This setting controls whether support interface being ironed. When enabled, support interface will be extruded as solid too.

support_ironing_pattern.label: Support Ironing Pattern
support_ironing_pattern.tooltip: The pattern that will be used when ironing.

support_ironing_flow.label: Support Ironing flow
support_ironing_flow.tooltip: The amount of material to extrude during ironing. Relative to flow of normal support interface layer height. Too high value results in overextrusion on the surface.

support_ironing_spacing.label: Support Ironing line spacing
support_ironing_spacing.tooltip: The distance between the lines of ironing.

support_ironing_speed.label: Support ironing speed
support_ironing_speed.tooltip: Print speed of the support ironing lines. 0 means the ironing speed.

support_ironing_inset.label: Support ironing inset
support_ironing_inset.tooltip: The distance to keep the support ironing lines from the edges of the ironed interface. 0 means no inset.

support_ironing_direction.label: Support ironing direction
support_ironing_direction.tooltip: Angle of the support ironing lines relative to the support interface lines.

over_support_surfaces.label: Over-support surfaces
over_support_surfaces.tooltip:
Print the object's bottom surfaces that rest on support material with their own flow and speed instead of the bridge settings.

With a top Z distance above 0 those surfaces are treated as bridges today, so they take Bridge flow ratio, Bridge speed, bridge density and Thick bridges - the same settings as a real unsupported span. They are not unsupported though, they are lying on the support interface, and they are usually the most visible faces of the print. Turn this on to print them like a bottom shell instead: the normal bottom surface pattern and density, no thick bridges, with Over-support flow and Over-support speed. True bridges over air are not affected.

The affected surfaces show up as "Bottom surface over support" in the preview's feature type view.

over_support_flow.label: Over-support flow
over_support_flow.tooltip:
Flow ratio for bottom surfaces that rest on support material, when "Over-support surfaces" is on.

1 means the normal flow for a solid layer of this height. Lower it a little if the surface over the support comes out rough or over-extruded; it replaces Bridge flow ratio for these surfaces.

over_support_speed.label: Over-support speed
over_support_speed.tooltip:
Print speed for bottom surfaces that rest on support material, when "Over-support surfaces" is on.

0 means follow the outer wall speed of the same layer, so the surface matches the walls around it - which is the point of the feature. Any other value is used as it is. It replaces Bridge speed for these surfaces.

support_top_z_distance.label: Top Z distance
support_top_z_distance.tooltip: Z gap between the support's top and object.

support_bottom_z_distance.label: Bottom Z distance
support_bottom_z_distance.tooltip: Z gap between the object and the support bottom. If Support Top Z Distance is 0 and the bottom has interface layers, this value is ignored and the support is printed in direct contact with the object (no gap).

tree_support_wall_count.label: Support wall loops
tree_support_wall_count.tooltip: This setting specifies the count of support walls in the range of [0,2]. 0 means auto.

support_base_pattern.label: Base pattern
support_base_pattern.tooltip:
Line pattern of support.

The Default option for Tree supports is Hollow, which means no base pattern. For other support types, the Default option is the Rectilinear pattern.

NOTE: For Organic supports, the two walls are supported only with the Hollow/Default base pattern. The Lightning base pattern is supported only by Tree Slim/Strong/Hybrid supports. For the other support types, the Rectilinear will be used instead of Lightning.

support_angle.label: Pattern angle
support_angle.tooltip: Use this setting to rotate the support pattern on the horizontal plane.

support_interface_pattern.label: Interface pattern
support_interface_pattern.tooltip: Line pattern of support interface. Default pattern for non-soluble support interface is Rectilinear, while default pattern for soluble support interface is Concentric.

support_interface_spacing.label: Top interface spacing
support_interface_spacing.tooltip:
Spacing of interface lines. Zero means solid interface.
Force using solid interface when support ironing is enabled.

support_bottom_interface_spacing.label: Bottom interface spacing
support_bottom_interface_spacing.tooltip: Spacing of bottom interface lines. Zero means solid interface.

support_expansion.label: Normal Support expansion
support_expansion.tooltip: Expand (+) or shrink (-) the horizontal span of normal support.

support_object_xy_distance.label: Support/object xy distance
support_object_xy_distance.tooltip: XY separation between an object and its support.

top_z_overrides_xy_distance.label: Z overrides X/Y
top_z_overrides_xy_distance.tooltip: When top z distance overrides support/object xy distance, give priority to ensuring that supports are generated beneath overhangs, and a gap of the same size as top z distance is leaved with the model. Whereas in the opposite case, the gap between supports and the model follows support/object xy distance all the time. Only recommended to enable when using HybridTree.

support_object_first_layer_gap.label: Support/object first layer gap
support_object_first_layer_gap.tooltip: XY separation between an object and its support at the first layer.

bridge_no_support.label: Don't support bridges
bridge_no_support.tooltip: Don't support the whole bridge area which make support very large. Bridges can usually be printed directly without support if not very long.

max_bridge_length.label: Max bridge length
max_bridge_length.tooltip: Max length of bridges that don't need support. Set it to 0 if you want all bridges to be supported, and set it to a very large value if you don't want any bridges to be supported.

independent_support_layer_height.label: Independent support layer height
independent_support_layer_height.tooltip: Support layer uses layer height independent with object layer. This is to support customizing z-gap and save print time. This option will be invalid when the prime tower is enabled.

tree_support_tip_diameter.label: Tip Diameter
tree_support_tip_diameter.tooltip: Branch tip diameter for organic supports.

tree_support_branch_distance.label: Tree support branch distance
tree_support_branch_distance.tooltip: This setting determines the distance between neighboring tree support nodes.

tree_support_branch_distance_organic.label: Tree support branch distance
tree_support_branch_distance_organic.tooltip: This setting determines the distance between neighboring tree support nodes.

tree_support_top_rate.label: Branch Density
tree_support_top_rate.tooltip: Adjusts the density of the support structure used to generate the tips of the branches. A higher value results in better overhangs but the supports are harder to remove, thus it is recommended to enable top support interfaces instead of a high branch density value if dense interfaces are needed.

tree_support_branch_diameter.label: Tree support branch diameter
tree_support_branch_diameter.tooltip: This setting determines the initial diameter of support nodes.

tree_support_branch_diameter_organic.label: Tree support branch diameter
tree_support_branch_diameter_organic.tooltip: This setting determines the initial diameter of support nodes.

tree_support_branch_diameter_angle.label: Branch Diameter Angle
tree_support_branch_diameter_angle.tooltip: The angle of the branches' diameter as they gradually become thicker towards the bottom. An angle of 0 will cause the branches to have uniform thickness over their length. A bit of an angle can increase stability of the organic support.

tree_support_branch_angle.label: Tree support branch angle
tree_support_branch_angle.tooltip: This setting determines the maximum overhang angle that the branches of tree support are allowed to make. If the angle is increased, the branches can be printed more horizontally, allowing them to reach farther.

tree_support_branch_angle_organic.label: Tree support branch angle
tree_support_branch_angle_organic.tooltip: This setting determines the maximum overhang angle that the branches of tree support are allowed to make. If the angle is increased, the branches can be printed more horizontally, allowing them to reach farther.

tree_support_angle_slow.label: Preferred Branch Angle
tree_support_angle_slow.tooltip: The preferred angle of the branches, when they do not have to avoid the model. Use a lower angle to make them more vertical and more stable. Use a higher angle for branches to merge faster.

tree_support_auto_brim.label: Auto brim width
tree_support_auto_brim.tooltip: Enabling this option means the width of the brim for tree support will be automatically calculated.

tree_support_brim_width.label: Tree support brim width
tree_support_brim_width.tooltip: Distance from tree branch to the outermost brim line.

stabilizer_supports.label: Side stabilizers
stabilizer_supports.tooltip:
Add thin struts that touch tall, slender parts on their sides with a small pinpoint tip and stand on the build plate next to it. They keep the part from wobbling while it prints and snap off at the tip afterwards. Printed with the support filament, speed and line width; Enable supports does not need to be on.

Off: no stabilizers.
Auto: rings of touch points up the part's height, plus any stabilizer points painted with the support painting tool.
Manual: only the painted stabilizer points.

stabilizer_ring_spacing.label: Stabilizer ring spacing
stabilizer_ring_spacing.tooltip: Height between two rings of side touch points. The first ring is this high above the plate.

stabilizer_points_per_ring.label: Touch points per ring
stabilizer_points_per_ring.tooltip: How many struts touch the part in each ring, spread evenly around it. Every ring uses the same angles, so each pillar carries one strut per ring.

stabilizer_tip_diameter.label: Stabilizer tip diameter
stabilizer_tip_diameter.tooltip: Diameter of the pinpoint tip where a strut touches the part. Smaller leaves a smaller mark but holds less; keep it at least about twice the line width.

stabilizer_tip_gap.label: Stabilizer tip gap
stabilizer_tip_gap.tooltip: Space left between each tip and the part. 0 makes the tips touch the part, which is what stabilizes it; a small gap leaves no mark but only catches the part once it starts to sway.

stabilizer_pillar_diameter.label: Stabilizer pillar diameter
stabilizer_pillar_diameter.tooltip: Diameter of the pillars that carry the tips down to the build plate. A pillar is never thinner than four support lines, two on each side.

stabilizer_max_island_width.label: Stabilize parts up to width
stabilizer_max_island_width.tooltip: Only sections of the part narrower than this get touch points, so a wide base under a thin spire stays unmarked. 0 means every section.

stabilizer_pillar_base_diameter.label: Stabilizer pillar base diameter
stabilizer_pillar_base_diameter.tooltip: Diameter of the stabilizer pillars at the build plate. Pillars taper from this diameter at the plate to the pillar diameter at their top, like tree supports, which makes tall pillars much stiffer. 0, or anything not larger than the pillar diameter, keeps the pillars straight.

stabilizer_bracing.label: Brace stabilizer pillars
stabilizer_bracing.tooltip: Tie neighbouring stabilizer pillars together with 45 degree diagonal braces wherever a pillar would otherwise stand unbraced for longer than the maximum unbraced height. Braces climb at 45 degrees from one pillar to the next, so they print without bridges, and never pass closer to the part than the support XY distance.

stabilizer_brace_max_unbraced.label: Max unbraced pillar height
stabilizer_brace_max_unbraced.tooltip: The longest stretch of a stabilizer pillar between two ties - the plate, a strut or a brace - before a brace is added. Also what the Auto column shape calls a long unbraced pillar.

stabilizer_brace_max_span.label: Max bracing span
stabilizer_brace_max_span.tooltip: Pillars farther apart than this (axis to axis) are never braced to each other. A brace rises as much as it spans, so a long span also needs a long stretch of both pillars.

stabilizer_column_shape.label: Stabilizer column shape
stabilizer_column_shape.tooltip:
Cross-section of the stabilizer pillars.

Round: round pillars.
Rounded rectangle: every pillar is a column with a filleted rectangular cross-section, like a prime tower, which is much stiffer than a thin round pillar.
Auto: round pillars, and a rounded-rectangle column for a pillar at least the column height tall that stands alone or still has a stretch longer than the max unbraced height.

stabilizer_column_width.label: Stabilizer column width
stabilizer_column_width.tooltip: Size of a rounded-rectangle column along its struts, towards the part. The column's side facing the part stays where a round pillar's would, so a wider column grows away from the part. Never less than the pillar diameter.

stabilizer_column_length.label: Stabilizer column length
stabilizer_column_length.tooltip: Size of a rounded-rectangle column across its struts, along the part's side. Never less than the pillar diameter.

stabilizer_column_min_height.label: Auto column height
stabilizer_column_min_height.tooltip: With the Auto column shape, only pillars at least this tall can become rounded-rectangle columns.

stabilizer_wall_loops.label: Stabilizer walls
stabilizer_wall_loops.tooltip: Number of walls around the stabilizer pillars, columns and braces, with sparse infill inside. 0 prints them solid. Parts too narrow for infill (thin pillars and the tips) always print solid.

stabilizer_infill_density.label: Stabilizer infill density
stabilizer_infill_density.tooltip: Density of the sparse infill inside the stabilizer walls. 100% prints them solid.

stabilizer_infill_pattern.label: Stabilizer infill pattern
stabilizer_infill_pattern.tooltip: Line pattern of the sparse infill inside the stabilizer walls.

enable_prime_tower.label: Enable
enable_prime_tower.tooltip: The wiping tower can be used to clean up the residue on the nozzle and stabilize the chamber pressure inside the nozzle, in order to avoid appearance defects when printing objects.

prime_volume.label: Prime volume
prime_volume.tooltip: The volume of material to prime extruder on tower.

prime_tower_brim_width.label: Brim width
prime_tower_brim_width.tooltip: Width of the brim. A negative value is the "auto" sentinel used by the Bambu Lab, Flashforge and Qidi process profiles: the brim then grows with the tower height (8 mm from 100 mm up).

prime_tower_brim_chamfer.label: Brim chamfer
prime_tower_brim_chamfer.tooltip: Enable gradual layer-by-layer reduction of the brim around the prime tower. This creates a chamfered/tapered effect, reducing material usage while maintaining first layer adhesion.

prime_tower_brim_chamfer_max_width.label: Max chamfer width
prime_tower_brim_chamfer_max_width.tooltip: Maximum width of the chamfer zone measured from the tower perimeter. The brim will reduce within this distance. Larger values create a more gradual taper but take more layers to complete.

wipe_tower_rotation_angle.label: Wipe tower rotation angle
wipe_tower_rotation_angle.tooltip:
Wipe tower rotation angle with respect to X axis. The tower turns about its front left corner; the Rotate tool (R) on the tower in the 3D view sets this angle too, turning the tower about its centre.
Not available for the Bambu Lab prime tower used on Bambu Lab printers, which is always printed unrotated.

wipe_tower_bridging.label: Maximal bridging distance
wipe_tower_bridging.tooltip: Maximal distance between supports on sparse infill sections.

wipe_tower_extra_spacing.label: Wipe tower purge lines spacing
wipe_tower_extra_spacing.tooltip: Spacing of purge lines on the wipe tower.

wipe_tower_extra_flow.label: Extra flow for purging
wipe_tower_extra_flow.tooltip: Extra flow used for the purging lines on the wipe tower. This makes the purging lines thicker or narrower than they normally would be. The spacing is adjusted automatically.

wipe_tower_max_purge_speed.label: Maximum wipe tower print speed of out wall
wipe_tower_max_purge_speed.tooltip: Maximum wipe tower print speed of out wall.

prime_tower_acceleration.label: Prime tower acceleration
prime_tower_acceleration.tooltip: The acceleration used for prime tower extrusions, with travels inside the tower at the travel acceleration. Does not affect the first layer. 0 means the tower sets no acceleration of its own. Bambu Lab printers (Type 1 tower) only.

prime_tower_line_width.label: Prime tower line width
prime_tower_line_width.tooltip: Line width of the prime tower walls, purge lines and brim. 0 means 1.25 times the nozzle diameter. Bambu Lab printers (Type 1 tower) only.

prime_tower_wipe_speed.label: Tool change wipe speed
prime_tower_wipe_speed.tooltip: Speed of the wipe before a tool change, on the way to the prime tower. 0 means the normal wipe speed.

prime_tower_wipe_distance.label: Tool change wipe distance
prime_tower_wipe_distance.tooltip: Length of the wipe before a tool change. 0 means the filament's wipe distance.

wipe_tower_wall_type.label: Wall type
wipe_tower_wall_type.tooltip:
Wipe tower outer wall type.
1. Rectangle: The default wall type, a rectangle with fixed width and height.
2. Cone: A cone with a fillet at the bottom to help stabilize the wipe tower.
3. Rib: Adds four ribs to the tower wall for enhanced stability.

wipe_tower_cone_angle.label: Stabilization cone apex angle
wipe_tower_cone_angle.tooltip: Angle at the apex of the cone that is used to stabilize the wipe tower. Larger angle means wider base.

wipe_tower_extra_rib_length.label: Extra rib length
wipe_tower_extra_rib_length.tooltip: Positive values can increase the size of the rib wall, while negative values can reduce the size. However, the size of the rib wall can not be smaller than that determined by the cleaning volume.

wipe_tower_fillet_wall.label: Fillet wall
wipe_tower_fillet_wall.tooltip: The wall of prime tower will fillet.

wipe_tower_no_sparse_layers.label: No sparse layers (beta)
wipe_tower_no_sparse_layers.tooltip: If enabled, the wipe tower will not be printed on layers with no tool changes. On layers with a tool change, extruder will travel downward to print the wipe tower, so the tower ends up below the model and the toolhead has to reach down to it. Layouts where that would collide with an already printed object are rejected. Has no effect with smooth timelapse, which needs a tower on every layer.

wipe_tower_sparse_layers_combination.label: Combine sparse layers
wipe_tower_sparse_layers_combination.tooltip:
If enabled, consecutive layers on which the prime tower has no filament change are printed as a single thicker tower layer instead of one thin layer each, the same way infill combination merges sparse infill. The merged layer is printed at the top of the run, at the height of everything it covers.

Only whole layers are merged, and never past the maximum layer height of the nozzle printing the tower (three quarters of the nozzle diameter when that is left at 0). Two or more layers therefore have to fit under that limit before anything changes at all: at a 0.2 mm layer height under a 0.3 mm maximum nothing is merged, while at 0.1 mm three layers become one.

Unlike "No sparse layers" the tower keeps following the model, so the toolhead never has to reach down to it. Has no effect with "No sparse layers" or smooth timelapse, which needs a tower on every layer.

wipe_tower_wall_gap.label: Wall gap
wipe_tower_wall_gap.tooltip: Create small gaps in the wipe tower outer wall at tool change entry points. The first extrusion path after a filament change will enter through the gap, leaving the filament blob on the gap edge instead of on the outer wall surface.

wipe_tower_stagger_toolchange_start.label: Stagger toolchange start
wipe_tower_stagger_toolchange_start.tooltip:
Vary the prime tower entry point for toolchange wiping between layers. This spreads startup ooze and ironing marks across several purge lines instead of stacking them at the same wall gap.
The tower's first layer, local-Z dithering tool changes, and tower-interface run-in changes keep the legacy start so the wall gap and the purge stay aligned.

wipe_tower_interface_temp.label: Heat up for tower interfaces
wipe_tower_interface_temp.tooltip: At a tower interface tool change, wait for the new filament's tower interface temperature (filament setting) before purging it on the prime tower, and set the normal nozzle temperature again right after the purge. A hotter first line bonds better onto a different material. Costs one heat-up wait per interface.

wipe_tower_interface_run_in.label: Run in from outside the tower
wipe_tower_interface_run_in.tooltip: At a tower interface tool change, start the purge the filament's tower interface run-in distance (filament setting) outside the side of the tower and extrude from there into it, so the blob that builds up while the pressure returns lands outside the tower instead of on it. The run-in line enters through a gap cut in the tower's outer wall on that layer and the three layers below, so it never drags across the wall: this needs "Wall gap" and does nothing without it. The prime tower's reserved area grows by the run-in distance, so objects and the skirt keep clear of the run-in; the start is also kept on the printable bed.

wipe_tower_interface_extra_prime.label: Extra prime at tower interfaces
wipe_tower_interface_extra_prime.tooltip: At a tower interface tool change, push extra filament through the standing nozzle before the purge to rebuild the pressure lost in the tool change: the filament's tower interface extra prime length plus 2 mm, as Bambu Studio does. With "Run in from outside the tower" the prime happens at the run-in start, outside the tower; otherwise at the start of the purge, in the wall gap when "Wall gap" is on.

wipe_tower_interface_trigger.label: Interface features apply on
wipe_tower_interface_trigger.tooltip:
Which prime tower tool changes count as a tower interface, where one material is purged onto a different one, for the three tower interface options below.
Every tool change: all of them.
Material change: the two filaments differ in filament type, or only one of them is a support filament.
Material family change: the two filaments belong to different material families (PLA and PLA-CF are one family, so are ABS and ASA, PETG and PCTG, the PA grades, TPU grades, PVA and BVOH; support filaments form their own family). This is closest to Bambu Studio, which applies its interface features where a different adhesion category starts on the tower.
The tower's first layer is never an interface.

single_extruder_multi_material_priming.label: Prime all printing extruders
single_extruder_multi_material_priming.tooltip: If enabled, all printing extruders will be primed at the front edge of the print bed at the start of the print.

preload_all_filaments.label: Preload all filaments
preload_all_filaments.tooltip: Loads every filament used on the plate during the first layer through the prime tower, so later colour changes do not pause mid-layer. Costs one purge per filament at the start of the print. Requires the prime tower.

outer_wall_filament.label: Outer wall
outer_wall_filament.tooltip: Filament to print outer walls. "Default" uses the Walls filament.

sparse_infill_filament.label: Infill
sparse_infill_filament.tooltip: Filament to print internal sparse infill.

wipe_tower_filament.label: Wipe tower
wipe_tower_filament.tooltip: The extruder to use when printing perimeter of the wipe tower. Set to 0 to use the one that is available (non-soluble would be preferred).

ooze_prevention.label: Enable
ooze_prevention.tooltip: This option will drop the temperature of the inactive extruders to prevent oozing.

standby_temperature_delta.label: Temperature variation
standby_temperature_delta.tooltip: Temperature difference to be applied when an extruder is not active. The value is not used when 'idle_temperature' in filament settings is set to non-zero value.

preheat_time.label: Preheat time
preheat_time.tooltip: To reduce the waiting time after tool change, Orca can preheat the next tool while the current tool is still in use. This setting specifies the time in seconds to preheat the next tool. Orca will insert a M104 command to preheat the tool in advance.

preheat_steps.label: Preheat steps
preheat_steps.tooltip: Insert multiple preheat commands (e.g. M104.1). Only useful for Prusa XL. For other printers, please set it to 1.

delta_temperature.label: Preheat delta temperature
delta_temperature.tooltip: Allow user to set the Preheat temperature. If target temperature is 220 and Preheat delta temperature is -30, then the preheat temperature will be 190

flush_into_infill.label: Flush into objects' infill
flush_into_infill.tooltip: Purging after filament change will be done inside objects' infills. This may lower the amount of waste and decrease the print time. If the walls are printed with transparent filament, the mixed color infill will be seen outside. It will not take effect, unless the prime tower is enabled.

flush_into_objects.label: Flush into this object
flush_into_objects.tooltip: This object will be used to purge the nozzle after a filament change to save filament and decrease the print time. Colors of the objects will be mixed as a result. It will not take effect unless the prime tower is enabled.

flush_into_support.label: Flush into objects' support
flush_into_support.tooltip: Purging after filament change will be done inside objects' support. This may lower the amount of waste and decrease the print time. It will not take effect, unless the prime tower is enabled. Ignored for an object whose Support interface filament source is set to Nearest wall - its support keeps the color already matched to it instead of being used for purging.

interlocking_beam.label: Use beam interlocking
interlocking_beam.tooltip: Generate interlocking beam structure at the locations where different filaments touch. This improves the adhesion between filaments, especially models printed in different materials.

toolchange_ordering.label: Toolchange ordering
toolchange_ordering.tooltip:
Determines the order of tool changes on each layer.
- Default: Starts with the last used extruder to minimize tool changes.
- Cyclic: Uses a fixed tool sequence each layer. This sacrifices speed for better surface quality, as the extra toolchanges allow layers more time to cool.

toolchange_cyclic_order.label: Cyclic order
toolchange_cyclic_order.tooltip:
Custom filament sequence used by the cyclic toolchange ordering, as filament numbers separated by commas (e.g. "3,2,1,4").
Each layer prints its filaments following this sequence; filaments not listed are printed last, in ascending order.
Leave empty to use the customized filament sequence set for the plate (Other layers filament sequence) when one exists, and to cycle through the filaments in ascending order otherwise.

toolchange_cyclic_first_layer.label: Apply cyclic order to first layer
toolchange_cyclic_first_layer.tooltip:
Applies the cyclic toolchange order to the first layer as well.
By default this is disabled, because the first layer is instead ordered for the best bed adhesion: filaments that print small, fragile first-layer features are printed last, so the following tool changes and travel moves are less likely to knock those weakly anchored parts loose. This first-layer order also honors a custom first layer filament sequence when one is set. The cyclic order's benefit (extra tool changes give each layer more time to cool) does not apply to the first layer, which is printed slowly and hot for adhesion.
Enable this only if you need the exact same tool sequence on every layer, including the first, at the cost of that adhesion optimization.

interface_shells.label: Interface shells
interface_shells.tooltip: Force the generation of solid shells between adjacent materials/volumes. Useful for multi-extruder prints with translucent materials or manual soluble support material.

enable_order_independent_overlap_carving.label: Order-independent overlap carving
enable_order_independent_overlap_carving.tooltip: When two normal parts of the same object overlap, the smaller part carves the larger one, no matter which order the parts appear in the object list. With this off the part listed later always carves the one listed earlier, so a small part sitting inside a bigger one is erased outright when it happens to be listed first. Useful for multi-body STEP imports, where the exporting CAD program decides the body order.

paint_depth_mode.label: Paint depth mode
paint_depth_mode.tooltip: Controls how thick a painted (multi-material/multi-color) claim is before the object reverts to its base filament for walls, solid infill and sparse infill. The depth is measured perpendicular to the painted surface, so it is the same on a vertical wall, on a curve and on a flat top. Without a bound, a small dark painted spot can extrude dark filament all the way to the object's core, showing through light-colored walls/infill above and around it. "Limited by distance" sets that thickness directly in millimeters and is the control to reach for; "Limited by walls" converts a wall count into the same millimeter thickness; "Unlimited" (the default) does not bound the painted claim, so it reaches the object's medial axis and the inside follows the paint.

paint_depth_walls.label: Paint depth walls
paint_depth_walls.tooltip: Thickness of a painted claim, expressed as a number of wall widths, when "Paint depth mode" is "Limited by walls". This is converted to about that many wall widths of material measured perpendicular to the painted surface: one perimeter spacing per wall, plus the inset the wall generator applies before laying its outer loop, plus a margin so the thickness does not sit on a rounding boundary. It is a thickness, not a promise of a loop count - how many loops fit inside it is decided by "Wall generator" (the classic generator tiles a band with an even number of loops plus a gap-fill line, and Arachne will not produce more than twice "Wall loops" loops in any region, so depth beyond that prints as painted solid/sparse infill). If you want an exact thickness in millimeters, use "Limited by distance" instead.

paint_depth_mm.label: Paint depth distance
paint_depth_mm.tooltip: How thick a painted claim is, measured perpendicular to the painted surface, when "Paint depth mode" is "Limited by distance". The same everywhere: a vertical wall gets this much colour measured horizontally, a flat top gets it measured vertically, and a slope gets it measured along its own normal - so a painted region behaves like a shell of the color rather than thinning out on shallow curves. Zero behaves the same as "Paint depth mode" = "Unlimited": no clamp is applied on any layer.

paint_infill_override.label: Paint sparse infill
paint_infill_override.tooltip: If enabled (default), a painted claim's sparse infill is printed in the painted filament, matching walls and solid infill. If disabled, a bounded painted claim ("Paint depth mode" other than "Unlimited") keeps its sparse infill in the object's base filament - walls and solid infill (which can be visible on top surfaces) still print in the painted filament.

paint_depth_solid_interfaces.label: Paint depth solid interfaces
paint_depth_solid_interfaces.tooltip: Print solid shells at colour boundaries inside the object so the base colour cannot show through painted areas from above/below. Turning this off saves solid material and time but can let the base colour bleed through thin painted skins.

mmu_segmented_region_interlocking_depth.label: Interlocking depth of a segmented region
mmu_segmented_region_interlocking_depth.tooltip: Interlocking depth of a segmented region. Only active when "Paint depth mode" is not "Unlimited". Zero disables this feature. When "Paint depth mode" is "Limited by walls", the effective depth is capped at a quarter of one perimeter spacing (about 0.11mm at a 0.45mm line width), because a deeper notch would narrow the painted band on alternating layers by more than a whole wall loop - so "Paint depth walls" would silently deliver one wall fewer on every other layer. That cap does not apply when "Paint depth mode" is "Limited by distance": the value there is used exactly as entered, and setting it large relative to "Paint depth distance" can narrow the band on alternating layers enough to cost a loop there too - keep it small relative to that depth if you want the same loop count on every layer.

interlocking_beam_width.label: Interlocking beam width
interlocking_beam_width.tooltip: The width of the interlocking structure beams.

interlocking_beam_layer_count.label: Interlocking beam layers
interlocking_beam_layer_count.tooltip: The height of the beams of the interlocking structure, measured in number of layers. Less layers is stronger, but more prone to defects.

interlocking_depth.label: Interlocking depth
interlocking_depth.tooltip: The distance from the boundary between filaments to generate interlocking structure, measured in cells. Too few cells will result in poor adhesion.

interlocking_boundary_avoidance.label: Interlocking boundary avoidance
interlocking_boundary_avoidance.tooltip: The distance from the outside of a model where interlocking structures will not be generated, measured in cells.

dithering_local_z_mode.label: Subdivide Mix Layer
dithering_local_z_mode.tooltip: Enable "Subdivide Mix Layer" for mixing areas. Layer height will be subdivided for better color mixing results.

dithering_local_z_whole_objects.label: Full domain
dithering_local_z_whole_objects.tooltip:
Experimental. Apply Local-Z thinning across whole mixed-color regions instead of limiting the effect strictly to painted mixed masks.

Only available when Subdivide Mix Layer is enabled.

dithering_local_z_infill.label: Apply subdivision to infill
dithering_local_z_infill.tooltip:
Experimental. When Subdivide Mix Layer is enabled, also apply the same subdivision to infill inside mixed-color areas.

This is enabled automatically with Subdivide Mix Layer. Turn it off to keep infill on the normal layer height.

It can improve internal color mixing, but may add toolchanges and affect infill behavior.

skirt_loops.label: Skirt loops
skirt_loops.tooltip: Number of loops for the skirt. Zero means disabling skirt.

skirt_type.label: Skirt type
skirt_type.tooltip: Combined - single skirt for all objects, Per object - individual object skirt.

min_skirt_length.label: Skirt minimum extrusion length
min_skirt_length.tooltip:
Minimum filament extrusion length in mm when printing the skirt. Zero means this feature is disabled.

Using a non-zero value is useful if the printer is set up to print without a prime line.
Final number of loops is not taking into account while arranging or validating objects distance. Increase loop number in such case.

skirt_distance.label: Skirt distance
skirt_distance.tooltip: The distance from the skirt to the brim or the object.

skirt_start_angle.label: Skirt start point
skirt_start_angle.tooltip: Angle from the object center to skirt start point. Zero is the most right position, counter clockwise is positive angle.

skirt_speed.label: Skirt speed
skirt_speed.tooltip: Speed of skirt, in mm/s. Zero means use default layer extrusion speed.

skirt_height.label: Skirt height
skirt_height.tooltip: How many layers of skirt. Usually only one layer.

draft_shield.label: Draft shield
draft_shield.tooltip:
A draft shield is useful to protect an ABS or ASA print from warping and detaching from print bed due to wind draft. It is usually needed only with open frame printers, i.e. without an enclosure.

Enabled = skirt is as tall as the highest printed object. Otherwise 'Skirt height' is used.
Note: With the draft shield active, the skirt will be printed at skirt distance from the object. Therefore, if brims are active it may intersect with them. To avoid this, increase the skirt distance value.

single_loop_draft_shield.label: Single loop after first layer
single_loop_draft_shield.tooltip: Limits the skirt/draft shield loops to one wall after the first layer. This is useful, on occasion, to conserve filament but may cause the draft shield/skirt to warp / crack.

brim_type.label: Brim type
brim_type.tooltip: This controls the generation of the brim at outer and/or inner side of models. Auto means the brim width is analyzed and calculated automatically.

brim_filament_source.label: Brim filament
brim_filament_source.tooltip: object: brim uses each object's filament (default). nearest_wall: each brim extrusion uses the filament of the nearest first-layer wall, so brims match what they touch (multi-filament prints only). Applies to by-layer printing; by-object (sequential) prints use the object's filament.

brim_width.label: Brim width
brim_width.tooltip: Distance from model to the outermost brim line.

brim_object_gap.label: Brim-object gap
brim_object_gap.tooltip: A gap between innermost brim line and object can make brim be removed more easily.

brim_flow_ratio.label: Brim flow ratio
brim_flow_ratio.tooltip:
This factor affects the amount of material for brims.

The actual brim flow used is calculated by multiplying this value by the filament flow ratio, and if set, the object's flow ratio.

brim_use_efc_outline.label: Brim follows compensated outline
brim_use_efc_outline.tooltip:
When enabled, the brim is aligned with the first-layer perimeter geometry after Elephant Foot Compensation is applied.
This option is intended for cases where Elephant Foot Compensation significantly alters the first-layer footprint.

If your current setup already works well, enabling it may be unnecessary and can cause the brim to fuse with upper layers.

combine_brims.label: Combine brims
combine_brims.tooltip: Combine multiple brims into one when they are close to each other. This can improve brim adhesion.

brim_ears_max_angle.label: Brim ear max angle
brim_ears_max_angle.tooltip:
Maximum angle to let a brim ear appear.
If set to 0, no brim will be created.
If set to ~180, brim will be created on everything but straight sections.

brim_ears_detection_length.label: Brim ear detection radius
brim_ears_detection_length.tooltip:
The geometry will be decimated before detecting sharp angles. This parameter indicates the minimum length of the deviation for the decimation.
0 to deactivate.

brim_ears_outer_only.label: Brim ears outer only
brim_ears_outer_only.tooltip: Generate mouse ears only on the outer contour of the model, excluding holes and enclosed sections.

slicing_mode.label: Slicing Mode
slicing_mode.tooltip: Use "Even-odd" for 3DLabPrint airplane models. Use "Close holes" to close all holes in the model.

print_sequence.label: Print sequence
print_sequence.tooltip: Print sequence, layer by layer or object by object.

print_order.label: Intra-layer order
print_order.tooltip: Print order within a single layer.

spiral_mode.label: Spiral vase
spiral_mode.tooltip: Spiralize smooths out the z moves of the outer contour. And turns a solid model into a single walled print with solid bottom layers. The final generated model has no seam.

spiral_mode_smooth.label: Smooth Spiral
spiral_mode_smooth.tooltip: Smooth Spiral smooths out X and Y moves as well, resulting in no visible seam at all, even in the XY directions on walls that are not vertical.

spiral_mode_max_xy_smoothing.label: Max XY Smoothing
spiral_mode_max_xy_smoothing.tooltip: Maximum distance to move points in XY to try to achieve a smooth spiral. If expressed as a %, it will be computed over nozzle diameter.

spiral_starting_flow_ratio.label: Spiral starting flow ratio
spiral_starting_flow_ratio.tooltip: Sets the starting flow ratio while transitioning from the last bottom layer to the spiral. Normally the spiral transition scales the flow ratio from 0% to 100% during the first loop which can in some cases lead to under extrusion at the start of the spiral.

spiral_finishing_flow_ratio.label: Spiral finishing flow ratio
spiral_finishing_flow_ratio.tooltip: Sets the finishing flow ratio while ending the spiral. Normally the spiral transition scales the flow ratio from 100% to 0% during the last loop which can in some cases lead to under extrusion at the end of the spiral.

timelapse_type.label: Timelapse
timelapse_type.tooltip: If smooth or traditional mode is selected, a timelapse video will be generated for each print. After each layer is printed, a snapshot is taken with the chamber camera. All of these snapshots are composed into a timelapse video when printing completes. If smooth mode is selected, the toolhead will move to the excess chute after each layer is printed and then take a snapshot. Since the melt filament may leak from the nozzle during the process of taking a snapshot, prime tower is required for smooth mode to wipe nozzle.

fuzzy_skin.label: Fuzzy Skin
fuzzy_skin.tooltip: Randomly jitter while printing the wall, so that the surface has a rough look. This setting controls the fuzzy position.

fuzzy_skin_mode.label: Fuzzy skin generator mode
fuzzy_skin_mode.tooltip:
Fuzzy skin generation mode. Works only with Arachne!
Displacement: Сlassic mode when the pattern is formed by shifting the nozzle sideways from the original path.
Extrusion: The mode when the pattern formed by the amount of extruded plastic. This is the fast and straight algorithm without unnecessary nozzle shake that gives a smooth pattern. But it is more useful for forming loose walls in the entire they array.
Combined: Joint mode [Displacement] + [Extrusion]. The appearance of the walls is similar to [Displacement] Mode, but it leaves no pores between the perimeters.

Attention! The [Extrusion] and [Combined] modes works only the fuzzy_skin_thickness parameter not more than the thickness of printed loop. At the same time, the width of the extrusion for a particular layer should also not be below a certain level. It is usually equal 15-25%% of a layer height. Therefore, the maximum fuzzy skin thickness with a perimeter width of 0.4 mm and a layer height of 0.2 mm will be 0.4-(0.2*0.25)=±0.35mm! If you enter a higher parameter than this, the error Flow::spacing() will displayed, and the model will not be sliced. You can choose this number until this error is repeated.

fuzzy_skin_noise_type.label: Fuzzy skin noise type
fuzzy_skin_noise_type.tooltip:
Noise type to use for fuzzy skin generation:
Classic: Classic uniform random noise.
Perlin: Perlin noise, which gives a more consistent texture.
Billow: Similar to perlin noise, but clumpier.
Ridged Multifractal: Ridged noise with sharp, jagged features. Creates marble-like textures.
Voronoi: Divides the surface into voronoi cells, and displaces each one by a random amount. Creates a patchwork texture.
Ripple: Uniform ripple pattern that ripples left and right of the original path. Repeating pattern, woven appearance.

fuzzy_skin_point_distance.label: Fuzzy skin point distance
fuzzy_skin_point_distance.tooltip: The average distance between the random points introduced on each line segment.

fuzzy_skin_thickness.label: Fuzzy skin thickness
fuzzy_skin_thickness.tooltip: The width within which to jitter. It's advised to be below outer wall line width.

fuzzy_skin_scale.label: Fuzzy skin feature size
fuzzy_skin_scale.tooltip: The base size of the coherent noise features, in mm. Higher values will result in larger features.

fuzzy_skin_octaves.label: Fuzzy Skin Noise Octaves
fuzzy_skin_octaves.tooltip: The number of octaves of coherent noise to use. Higher values increase the detail of the noise, but also increase computation time.

fuzzy_skin_persistence.label: Fuzzy skin noise persistence
fuzzy_skin_persistence.tooltip: The decay rate for higher octaves of the coherent noise. Lower values will result in smoother noise.

fuzzy_skin_ripples_per_layer.label: Number of ripples per layer
fuzzy_skin_ripples_per_layer.tooltip: Controls how many full cycles of ripples will be added per layer.

fuzzy_skin_ripple_offset.label: Ripple offset
fuzzy_skin_ripple_offset.tooltip:
Shifts the ripple phase forward along the print path by the specified percentage of a wavelength each layer period.
- 0% keeps every layer identical.
- 50% shifts the pattern by half a wavelength, effectively inverting the phase.
- 100% shifts the pattern by a full wavelength, returning to the original phase.

The shift is applied once every number of layers set by Layers between ripple offset, so layers within the same group are printed identically.

fuzzy_skin_layers_between_ripple_offset.label: Layers between ripple offset
fuzzy_skin_layers_between_ripple_offset.tooltip:
Specifies how many consecutive layers share the same ripple phase before the offset is applied.
For example:
- 1 = Layer 1 is printed with the base ripple pattern, then layer 2 is shifted by the configured offset, then layer 3 returns to the base pattern, and so on.
- 3 = Layers 1 to 3 are printed with the base ripple pattern, then layers 4 to 6 are shifted by the configured offset, then layers 7 to 9 return to the base pattern, etc.

fuzzy_skin_first_layer.label: Apply fuzzy skin to first layer
fuzzy_skin_first_layer.tooltip: Whether to apply fuzzy skin on the first layer.

fuzzy_skin_skip_overhangs.label: Skip fuzzy skin on overhangs
fuzzy_skin_skip_overhangs.tooltip: Do not apply fuzzy skin to the parts of a wall that are not supported by the layer below. Overhanging and bridging wall segments keep their original, unfuzzed path, so the jitter does not push extrusion out into open air where it would curl. The displacement is faded out over a couple of sample points on either side of the boundary, so there is no step between the fuzzed and the clean part of the wall. The first layer is never treated as an overhang.

reduce_infill_retraction.label: Reduce infill retraction
reduce_infill_retraction.tooltip: Don't retract when the travel is in infill area absolutely. That means the oozing can't been seen. This can reduce times of retraction for complex model and save printing time, but make slicing and G-code generating slower.

gcode_add_line_number.label: Add line number
gcode_add_line_number.tooltip: Enable this to add line number(Nx) at the beginning of each G-code line.

gcode_comments.label: Verbose G-code
gcode_comments.tooltip: Enable this to get a commented G-code file, with each line explained by a descriptive text. If you print from SD card, the additional weight of the file could make your firmware slow down.

gcode_label_objects.label: Label objects
gcode_label_objects.tooltip: Enable this to add comments into the G-code labeling print moves with what object they belong to, which is useful for the Octoprint CancelObject plugin. This settings is NOT compatible with Single Extruder Multi Material setup and Wipe into Object / Wipe into Infill.

exclude_object.label: Exclude objects
exclude_object.tooltip: Enable this option to add EXCLUDE OBJECT command in G-code.

exclude_object_tolerance.label: Outline tolerance
exclude_object_tolerance.tooltip: Maximum deviation of the object outline written to EXCLUDE_OBJECT_DEFINE from the original outline. Larger values give fewer points, which helps firmware that stalls while parsing G-code with many objects. 0 keeps every point. The points are rounded to 0.1 mm either way.

filename_format.label: Filename format
filename_format.tooltip: Users can define the project file name when exporting.

process_change_extrusion_role_gcode.label: Change extrusion role G-code (process)
process_change_extrusion_role_gcode.tooltip: This G-code is inserted when the extrusion role is changed. It runs after the machine and filament extrusion role G-code.

post_process.label: Post-processing Scripts
post_process.tooltip: If you want to process the output G-code through custom scripts, just list their absolute paths here. Separate multiple scripts with a semicolon. Scripts will be passed the absolute path to the G-code file as the first argument, and they can access the EdgeSlicer config settings by reading environment variables.

notes.label: Configuration notes
notes.tooltip: You can put here your personal notes. This text will be added to the G-code header comments.

lines.label: Recommended nozzle temperature
lines.tooltip: Recommended nozzle temperature range of this filament. 0 means no set

lines.label: Chamber temperature
lines.tooltip: Target chamber temperature, and the minimal chamber temperature at which printing should start

lines.label: Cool Plate
lines.tooltip: Bed temperature when this plate is installed. A value of 0 means the filament does not support printing on this plate.

lines.label: Textured Cool Plate
lines.tooltip: Bed temperature when this plate is installed. A value of 0 means the filament does not support printing on this plate.

lines.label: Engineering Plate
lines.tooltip: Bed temperature when this plate is installed. A value of 0 means the filament does not support printing on this plate.

filament_vendor.label: Vendor
filament_vendor.tooltip: Vendor of filament. For show only.

filament_soluble.tooltip: Soluble material is commonly used to print supports and support interfaces.

filament_is_support.tooltip: Support material is commonly used to print supports and support interfaces.

required_nozzle_HRC.label: Required nozzle HRC
required_nozzle_HRC.tooltip: Minimum HRC of nozzle required to print the filament. Zero means no checking of nozzle's HRC.

default_filament_colour.label: Default color
default_filament_colour.tooltip:
Default filament color.
Right click to reset value to system default.

filament_diameter.label: Diameter
filament_diameter.tooltip: Filament diameter is used to calculate extrusion in G-code, so it is important and should be accurate.

filament_shrink.label: Shrinkage (XY)
filament_shrink.tooltip:
Enter the shrinkage percentage that the filament will get after cooling (94% if you measure 94mm instead of 100mm). The part will be scaled in xy to compensate. Only the filament used for the perimeter is taken into account.
Be sure to allow enough space between objects, as this compensation is done after the checks.

filament_shrinkage_compensation_z.label: Shrinkage (Z)
filament_shrinkage_compensation_z.tooltip: Enter the shrinkage percentage that the filament will get after cooling (94% if you measure 94mm instead of 100mm). The part will be scaled in Z to compensate.

filament_z_offset.label: Filament Z offset
filament_z_offset.tooltip: Added to the printer's Z offset when printing with this filament. Useful for per-filament squish or textured/smooth plate differences without editing the printer profile. Applied for the first printing filament of a job.

temperature_vitrification.label: Softening temperature
temperature_vitrification.tooltip: The material softens at this temperature, so when the bed temperature is equal to or greater than this, it's highly recommended to open the front door and/or remove the upper glass to avoid clogging.

fins_extrude_safe_temp.label: Fin extrude safe temperature
fins_extrude_safe_temp.tooltip: Safe hotend temperature for fin extrusion. 0 means disabled. Accessible in custom G-code via fins_extrude_safe_temp.

idle_temperature.label: Idle temperature
idle_temperature.tooltip: Nozzle temperature when the tool is currently not used in multi-tool setups. This is only used when 'Ooze prevention' is active in Print Settings. Set to 0 to disable.

filament_cooling_before_tower.label: Wipe tower cooling
filament_cooling_before_tower.tooltip: Temperature drop before entering filament tower

filament_tower_ironing_area.label: Tower ironing area
filament_tower_ironing_area.tooltip: Ironing area for prime tower interface layer (where different materials meet).

pellet_flow_coefficient.label: Pellet flow coefficient
pellet_flow_coefficient.tooltip:
Pellet flow coefficient is empirically derived and allows for volume calculation for pellet printers.

Internally it is converted to filament_diameter. All other volume calculations remain the same.

filament_diameter = sqrt( (4 * pellet_flow_coefficient) / PI )

filament_flow_ratio.label: Flow ratio
filament_flow_ratio.tooltip: The material may have volumetric change after switching between molten and crystalline states. This setting changes all extrusion flow of this filament in G-code proportionally. The recommended value range is between 0.95 and 1.05. You may be able to tune this value to get a nice flat surface if there is slight overflow or underflow.

enable_pressure_advance.label: Enable pressure advance
enable_pressure_advance.tooltip: Enable pressure advance, auto calibration result will be overwritten once enabled.

pressure_advance.label: Pressure advance
pressure_advance.tooltip: Pressure advance (Klipper) AKA Linear advance factor (Marlin).

adaptive_pressure_advance.label: Enable adaptive pressure advance (beta)
adaptive_pressure_advance.tooltip:
With increasing print speeds (and hence increasing volumetric flow through the nozzle) and increasing accelerations, it has been observed that the effective PA value typically decreases. This means that a single PA value is not always 100% optimal for all features and a compromise value is usually used that does not cause too much bulging on features with lower flow speed and accelerations while also not causing gaps on faster features.

This feature aims to address this limitation by modeling the response of your printer's extrusion system depending on the volumetric flow speed and acceleration it is printing at. Internally, it generates a fitted model that can extrapolate the needed pressure advance for any given volumetric flow speed and acceleration, which is then emitted to the printer depending on the current print conditions.

When enabled, the pressure advance value above is overridden. However, a reasonable default value above is strongly recommended to act as a fallback and for when tool changing.

adaptive_pressure_advance_overhangs.label: Enable adaptive pressure advance within features (beta)
adaptive_pressure_advance_overhangs.tooltip:
Enable adaptive PA whenever there are flow changes in a feature, such as line width changes in a corner or overhangs.

Not compatible with Prusa printers as they pause to process PA changes, which causes delays and defects.

This is an experimental option, as if the PA profile is not set accurately, it will cause uniformity issues.

adaptive_pressure_advance_bridges.label: Static pressure advance for bridges
adaptive_pressure_advance_bridges.tooltip:
Static pressure advance value for bridges. Set to 0 to apply the same pressure advance as equivalent walls (using adaptive settings if enabled).

A lower PA value when printing bridges helps reduce the appearance of slight under-extrusion immediately after bridges. This is caused by the pressure drop in the nozzle when printing in the air and a lower PA helps counteract this.

adaptive_pressure_advance_model.label: Adaptive pressure advance measurements (beta)
adaptive_pressure_advance_model.tooltip:
Add sets of pressure advance (PA) values, the volumetric flow speeds and accelerations they were measured at, separated by a comma. One set of values per line. For example
0.04,3.96,3000
0.033,3.96,10000
0.029,7.91,3000
0.026,7.91,10000

How to calibrate:
1. Run the pressure advance test for at least 3 speeds per acceleration value. It is recommended that the test is run for at least the speed of the external perimeters, the speed of the internal perimeters and the fastest feature print speed in your profile (usually its the sparse or solid infill). Then run them for the same speeds for the slowest and fastest print accelerations, and no faster than the recommended maximum acceleration as given by the Klipper input shaper
2. Take note of the optimal PA value for each volumetric flow speed and acceleration. You can find the flow number by selecting flow from the color scheme drop down and move the horizontal slider over the PA pattern lines. The number should be visible at the bottom of the page. The ideal PA value should be decreasing the higher the volumetric flow is. If it is not, confirm that your extruder is functioning correctly. The slower and with less acceleration you print, the larger the range of acceptable PA values. If no difference is visible, use the PA value from the faster test
3. Enter the triplets of PA values, Flow and Accelerations in the text box here and save your filament profile

activate_chamber_temp_control.label: Activate temperature control
activate_chamber_temp_control.tooltip:
Enable this option for automated chamber temperature control. This option activates the emitting of an M191 command before the "machine_start_gcode"
 which sets the chamber temperature and waits until it is reached. In addition, it emits an M141 command at the end of the print to turn off the chamber heater, if present.

This option relies on the firmware supporting the M191 and M141 commands either via macros or natively and is usually used when an active chamber heater is installed.

chamber_temperature.label: Chamber temperature
chamber_temperature.tooltip:
For high-temperature materials like ABS, ASA, PC, and PA, a higher chamber temperature can help suppress or reduce warping and potentially lead to higher interlayer bonding strength. However, at the same time, a higher chamber temperature will reduce the efficiency of air filtration for ABS and ASA.

For PLA, PETG, TPU, PVA, and other low-temperature materials, this option should be disabled (set to 0) as the chamber temperature should be low to avoid extruder clogging caused by material softening at the heat break.

If enabled, this parameter also sets a G-code variable named chamber_temperature, which can be used to pass the desired chamber temperature to your print start macro, or a heat soak macro like this: PRINT_START (other variables) CHAMBER_TEMP=[chamber_temperature]. This may be useful if your printer does not support M141/M191 commands, or if you desire to handle heat soaking in the print start macro if no active chamber heater is installed.

chamber_minimal_temperature.label: Minimal
chamber_minimal_temperature.tooltip:
This is the chamber temperature at which printing should start, while the chamber continues heating toward the "Target" chamber temperature. For example, set the Target to 60 and the Minimal to 50 to begin printing once the chamber reaches 50℃, without waiting for the full 60℃.

It sets a G-code variable named chamber_minimal_temperature, which can be passed to your print start macro or a heat soak macro, like this: PRINT_START (other variables) CHAMBER_MIN_TEMP=[chamber_minimal_temperature].

Unlike the "Target" chamber temperature, this option does not emit any M141/M191 commands; it only exposes the value to your custom G-code. It should not exceed the "Target" chamber temperature.
